Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Authority Presence: Police, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted

Vignette:
Ravi is a 41-year-old graphic designer who has been married for twelve years. He comes to therapy because his wife told him she cannot watch him like this anymore—always looking over his shoulder, never agreeing to weekend plans, and spending hours in his home office rehearsing conversations with clients out loud before he can bring himself to call them. The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago, during a routine traffic stop on his way home from a late deadline at the studio.

He was driving through a suburban intersection when a patrol car’s lights flashed behind him. Ravi pulled over, certain it was a mistake—he had not been speeding, his registration was current. The officer approached, a young man in a crisp uniform, and asked for his license and registration. Ravi handed them over and began to explain that he had just come from work, that he was a graphic designer, that perhaps there was some confusion. The officer’s tone shifted rapidly. He accused Ravi of being argumentative, ordered him out of the car, and within seconds Ravi was on the pavement, his face against the asphalt, his hands cuffed behind his back. He heard a sharp click and then a burning, acrid smell filled his nostrils—something electrical, like ozone and melted plastic. Later he learned it was a taser being deployed against someone else at a nearby stop, but in that moment he believed it was for him. He lay there, unable to speak, while the officer berated him. The betrayal was absolute: he had trusted that uniform, that authority, and it had turned on him without cause.

After the incident, Ravi was released with a warning, but he did not feel released. The memory arrives not as a story he can tell but as a wave of guilt—he should have said something different, should have stayed calmer, should have prevented the whole thing. Yet when he tries to describe what happened to his wife or to a therapist, the words vanish. He knows exactly what took place, but his mouth goes dry and his mind blanks, and he trails off mid-sentence, unable to finish. The burnt smell returns without warning—from a passing car’s exhaust, from a neighbor’s grill—and he freezes, heart pounding, scanning for a uniform that might be coming for him.

Ravi’s work as a graphic designer once meant collaborating with clients, presenting ideas, and sketching out future campaigns. Now he refuses to plan anything beyond the immediate week. Making a future plan feels like inviting disaster: if he commits to a vacation or a project deadline, something terrible will happen. He spends hours in his home office, role-playing every possible conversation with a client before he can press dial. At the local coffee shop he keeps his back to the wall and watches the door, cataloging anyone who might be a dangerous person—someone in cargo pants, someone with a stern expression, anyone who moves too quickly. When he sees a police car, he turns down a side street or pulls into a parking lot until it passes. His wife has noticed he no longer visits his brother, who lives near a precinct.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was a moment in a grocery store. A security guard in a blue uniform walked past the cereal aisle, and Ravi dropped his basket and walked out without buying anything. He stood in the parking lot, shaking, unable to go back inside. That night his wife told him he could not go on like this. Ravi agreed, but what he is most afraid of is that he will never trust anyone again—that the world really is as dangerous as it feels now, and that the people he thought were safe were never safe at all. He hopes, cautiously, that talking about it might somehow give him back the words he lost that night on the pavement.
